newsitem.title: USA: Father offers to drop claim for Simpson confession.
newsitem.headline: Father offers to drop claim for Simpson confession.

text.p: Fred Goldman offered on Wednesday to give up all claims to the multimillion-dollar verdict he won against O.J. Simpson if the former football star confesses to killing Goldman's son.

"If the person whose name I don't use that murdered my son wants to write out a complete confession and publish it in newspapers around the country, we'll be glad to ignore the judgment," Goldman said in a radio interview.

A jury in Simpson's wrongful death civil trial last week blamed him for the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman. It awarded compensatory damages of $8.5 million to be shared by Goldman's divorced parents.
After a second round of deliberations, jurors on Monday added $12.5 million in punitive damages for Goldman's relatives and an equal sum for the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson.

Fred Goldman, who pursued the civil case against Simpson with fierce tenacity, said in an interview with the Salem Radio Network, a national broadcaster, that he did not care about the money but about assigning blame for his son's murder.

However, he said he did not expect Simpson to agree to his terms. "That'll never happen, never going to happen," Goldman said. "This person hasn't (taken) full responsibility for any of his actions in his lifetime."
Simpson, who has steadfastly maintained his innocence, was cleared of murder charges in a 1995 criminal trial.
Neither Simpson nor his attorneys were available for comment on Goldman's offer.

Goldman has always insisted that the civil trial was a "search for justice." At a post-trial news conference on Monday, he said: "The money is not an issue. It never has been. It's holding the man who killed my son and Nicole responsible."
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki put the damage awards on hold for 10 days to give Simpson lead attorney Robert Baker time to challenge the verdict.
Baker has not spoken to the media since the verdicts but legal analysts expect him to ask for a retrial and appeal if Fujisaki denies the motion.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs are expected to file a motion asking Fujisaki to sign a document putting the judgment into effect, at which time they can start going after Simpson's money and his possessions, including his mansion and his luxury Bentley car.
Baker claimed in court that Simpson was virtually broke and that his net worth was a negative $800,000 even before the damage awards.
But Daniel Petrocelli, Goldman's lawyer, contended that Simpson was worth more than $15 million and had the potential to earn between $2 million and $3 million a year by cashing in on his notoriety.
